title: Distributed Locks and Fencing Tokens: Why Naive Leases Break Under Process Pauses and How to Prevent Split-Brain Writes
summary: In distributed architectures, engineers frequently use distributed locks to ensure only one worker mutates a shared resource at a time—often reaching for Redis SETNX or Redlock. However, time-based leases harbor a critical failure mode: if an active worker experiences a Stop-The-World garbage collection pause, OS page fault, or network delay, its lease silently expires. When a second worker acquires the lock, both processes operate concurrently, triggering split-brain data corruption. Fencing tokens eliminate this vulnerability by attaching a monotonically increasing sequence number to every lock grant, enabling the underlying storage system to safely reject writes from outdated, zombie clients.
analogyTitle: The Real-Life Analogy: The Hotel Room Keycard vs. The Digital Door Reader with Monotonic Revision Codes
analogy:
Imagine checking into a hotel room where your digital keycard is scheduled to expire at 11:00 AM on checkout day. At 10:55 AM, you take the elevator down to grab ice, but the elevator gets stuck between floors for 20 minutes (the real-world equivalent of a Stop-The-World garbage collection pause or network delay).

At 11:00 AM, the front desk computer assumes you have checked out, clears the reservation, and issues a new keycard (Card #43) to the next arriving guest, who enters Room 402 and hangs their coat in the closet.

At 11:15 AM, technicians fix the elevator. You emerge, walk back to Room 402, and approach the door holding your old keycard (Card #42). If the door lock only verified whether your card was once valid or relied on an uncalibrated clock, you would walk straight in and dump your dirty laundry onto the new guest's bed! Both guests believe they hold the exclusive lease to the room.

Modern hotel keycard systems prevent this with monotonic sequence numbers (fencing tokens). When the front desk issued Card #43, it encoded the integer 43 into the card chip. The instant Card #43 touches the door reader, the door permanently ratchets its internal minimum token to 43. When you show up with Card #42, the door reader compares the tokens: 42 is less than 43, so the latch remains firmly locked. Even though your worker had no idea its lease expired while frozen in the elevator, the storage layer (the door) protected the room from split-brain contamination.

sections.heading: 1. The Illusion of Mutual Exclusion: How Asynchronous Networks Break Time-Based Leases
2. Fencing Tokens: Enforcing Correctness at the Storage Boundary
sections.content:
In his seminal analysis of distributed mutual exclusion, Martin Kleppmann identified a fundamental rule: A lock manager alone cannot guarantee safety. True mutual exclusion requires cooperation between the lock provider and the storage resource.

The solution is a fencing token—a monotonically increasing integer assigned whenever a lock is granted:

1. Token Assignment: When Worker 1 acquires the lock, the lock manager assigns token 34. When Worker 2 later acquires the lock, the lock manager assigns token 35.
2. Carrying the Token: Every write request to the database, object store, or file system must include this token: storage.write(data, fencingToken).
3. Storage-Level Validation: The storage service tracks the highest token it has processed (max_token_seen). When a write arrives, the storage engine compares tokens:

-- Storage-level atomic CAS / conditional update
UPDATE invoices 
SET data = $1, last_fencing_token = 35
WHERE id = 101 AND last_fencing_token < 35;

Now trace the failure scenario with fencing enabled: Worker 1 gets token 34 and freezes. Worker 2 gets token 35 and successfully updates the invoice; the database records last_fencing_token = 35. When Worker 1 unfreezes and attempts to write with token 34, the database evaluates 34 < 35, immediately rejects the write, and returns a concurrency conflict error. Worker 2's data remains pristine.

sections.heading: 3. Choosing the Right Tool: Redis Redlock vs. Consensus-Backed Stores (etcd & ZooKeeper)
sections.content:
Depending on the blast radius of a split-brain write, backend systems use different locking architectures:

• Single Redis Instance vs. Redlock: A single Redis instance using SET NX PX and a Lua script for atomic release is fast and sufficient for non-critical workloads (e.g., deduplicating email deliveries or preventing cache stampedes). Redlock attempts to achieve fault-tolerant locking across 5 independent Redis masters using quorum voting. However, Redlock relies heavily on physical wall clocks (system time elapsed across independent nodes). If an NTP clock step occurs or a node freezes during network transmission, Redlock's safety invariants degrade.
• Consensus-Backed Locks (etcd & ZooKeeper): When data corruption cannot be tolerated (e.g., primary database failover, leader election, or financial ledger allocation), production systems rely on strongly consistent CP datastores built on Raft or Paxos.
• In Apache ZooKeeper, clients create ephemeral sequential znodes. The node with the lowest sequence number holds the lock, and subsequent workers watch the immediate predecessor node, avoiding thundering herds.
• In etcd, locks are tied to heartbeated leases backed by Raft consensus. etcd provides a 64-bit mod_revision that increments on every store mutation. This revision number functions naturally as a built-in fencing token for downstream storage systems, delivering deterministic safety regardless of GC pauses or network timing.

takeaway: Distributed locks that rely solely on time-based lease expiration cannot guarantee mutual exclusion because network latency, garbage collection pauses, and clock drift can cause leases to expire while a client is still actively working. To achieve true correctness, distributed systems rely on fencing tokens—monotonically increasing numbers issued by the lock service. By verifying that each incoming write carries a token higher than any previously seen, the storage layer safely fences out zombie clients and prevents split-brain writes, turning fragile time assumptions into deterministic logical ordering.
